title: Children and death
hook: children do best with plain, honest words

segments.voice: Yesterday, the grief that starts while someone is still alive, and a king who fasted, then rose. Your line was before and after. Which carer did you go gently with? Day eight hundred three.

A small boy is told that Grandpa went to sleep and won't wake up. That night, he won't get into bed. He fights it, crying, and nobody can work out why, until someone finally asks him, and he says he doesn't want to go to sleep like Grandpa. Across town, a little girl hears that the family lost Grandma, and she wants to know why nobody is out looking for her. The grown-ups chose soft words to protect them. The children took the words at their word. Today, how to talk with children about death.
screen: `GRANDPA WENT TO SLEEP.` → `THE BOY WON'T GO TO BED.` → `WHY ISN'T ANYONE LOOKING FOR GRANDMA?`

segments.voice: First, say died. Organizations that support grieving children, such as the Dougy Center in Portland, Oregon, advise using the real words, died and dead, and then explaining what they mean in a way a child can hold: the body stopped working. It doesn't breathe, eat, or feel pain anymore, and it can't start again. It sounds harsh to adult ears. To a child, it's something solid to stand on. Second, why the soft words can backfire. Young children can take words literally. Asleep can make bedtime frightening. Lost suggests someone could be found. Went away can sound like a choice, or leave a child waiting at the window. The kindness meant by the soft word can turn into fear or confusion. Third, short, honest, and again. Children may ask the same question many times, sometimes days apart, and may play happily one minute and cry the next. That's not a sign they didn't understand. They're taking it in a bit at a time. The guidance is to answer briefly, truthfully, as many times as it's asked, and to say I don't know when you don't. Fourth, beliefs beside the fact, not instead of it. Families hold different beliefs about what follows death: heaven, rebirth, a return to God, or that nobody knows. Child grief guidance suggests sharing your family's beliefs alongside the plain fact. Grandma died. Her body stopped working. And then: here's what our family believes. The fact first, the belief beside it. Plain words.
screen: `SAY "DIED"` · `SOFT WORDS CAN FRIGHTEN` · `SHORT, HONEST, AND AGAIN` · `BELIEFS BESIDE THE FACT` · then, large: `PLAIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Think of a death a child in your life might ask about: a grandparent, a neighbor, a goldfish. Settle, and quietly shape one sentence a child could understand: the name, the word died, and one plain thing. Her body stopped working, so she can't come back. Say it slowly in your head. Notice any urge to soften it, and let the urge pass. Then add one warm, true line after it, such as we loved her, and we'll keep remembering her. Rest with the two sentences together. The bell holds the time.
Dougy Center, the organization that advises telling children the truth in plain words, died and dead, with warmth and room for questions. Today's word.
Your line: plain words. Today, notice one soft phrase you use for death, passed, lost, gone, and try the plain one at least once, even just in your head. Day eight hundred three.

howItsDone: Children's grief centers and hospice programs coach parents to use the words died and dead, explain that the body has stopped working, answer questions briefly and honestly, and share the family's beliefs alongside the facts.

match.prompt: soft word, what a child hears — tap the pairs.

myth: telling a child Grandpa went to sleep is the gentlest choice
it can make bedtime frightening; children take words at their word.
it's all right to tell a child "I don't know"
the guidance is to answer briefly and truthfully, including I don't know.
families should keep their beliefs out of it
the guidance suggests sharing beliefs beside the plain fact, not instead of it.

fork.setup: a small child looks up at you and asks, "is Grandpa sleeping?" what do you say?
options: "yes, he's sleeping for a very long time."
"no. Grandpa died. his body stopped working."
fork.reveal: plain words first, then stay for the next question, and the one after that. that's what grief guidance for children advises.

trapdoor: what you thought: protecting children means softening the words about death.
what it means: children do best with plain words, died and dead, said warmly and repeated as often as asked.
what a scholar hears: child bereavement guidance separates the fact (the body stopped working) from beliefs, and asks for both, fact first.

sources.ref: The Dougy Center (Portland, Oregon), guidance on talking with children about death

notes: Advice summarized from children's grief organizations (the Dougy Center named as an example). Verify the Dougy Center's published guidance says to use 'died' and explain the body stopped working.
'Young children can take words literally' is a general claim from that guidance; soften if it can't be sourced.
'Children may ask the same question many times' — 'many' here is about repetition, not a population claim.
No religious text cited; the day is practical. Beliefs listed (heaven, rebirth, a return to God, nobody knows) are named without ranking.
